title: Dept. of Health Molokai Town Hall Meeting: December 3, 2024

recap.headline: State pilot to fly Molokaʻi patients and doctors for non-emergency care
recap.in_60_seconds: The State Department of Health held a town hall on Molokaʻi with the area's State Senator and State Representative to gather input on a $2 million pilot to fly patients off-island and bring providers to Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi for non-emergency care. About 15 community members spoke or asked questions, and more questions came in by QR code. Health staff said the request for proposals should go out on eHawaii.gov at the end of December 2024, with an award in the first quarter of 2025 and the pilot running through 2026. The money will be split between the two islands by population and need. Molokaʻi's exact share, who will run the program, and how insurance reimbursement will work are still undecided. Residents were asked to fill out the online survey by Friday.

parts.title: Welcome and purpose
presented: The pilot aims to make non-emergency health care easier to reach through reliable air travel for Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi residents.
This is the first time the department has run a project like this, and many details are still unknown.
Questions can be sent by QR code during the meeting.

parts.title: Remarks from State legislators
presented: The Legislature set aside $2 million for a Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi medical travel pilot.
Community priorities will go into a request for proposals that private or nonprofit groups can bid on.
The meeting is not meant for complaints about Mokulele; the operator will need to work with several carriers.
If the pilot works, legislators hope to justify more funding.

parts.title: Pilot project details
presented: About $1.8 million is usable after a 20 percent holdback, split between the islands by population and need.
The department will hire outside entities, ideally one on each island, to run it, buy plane seats, and coordinate with providers and health plans.
Coverage is gate to gate only, with no ground transportation; a companion needs a provider's signed authorization.
The RFP is planned for the end of this month, with an award in the first quarter of 2025 and the pilot running through 2026.

next.what: Request for proposals posted on eHawaii.gov
Pilot runs and final reports go to the department and Legislature

parts.title: Molokaʻi Caires survey results
presented: The survey drew 270 responses in six months.
89 percent faced significant delays and 86 percent rescheduled or canceled an appointment because of travel problems.
Over 80 percent would use a specialist who came to Molokaʻi; almost 70 percent felt stressed about medical air travel.
37.4 percent needed two to four weeks to arrange travel.

parts.title: Questions: funding, backup travel and emergencies

raised.concern: How much of the money will go to Molokaʻi.
What happens when air travel goes down, since Lānaʻi has ferries.
Molokaʻi has no surgical capacity, so emergencies such as difficult births or patients too unstable to move have no solution.
Whether ferries or other non-air options are being studied, given delays reaching tests like ultrasounds.
What happens if a medical emergency occurs during a flight.

answered.said: Molokaʻi's share is not yet set; about $1.8 million is usable and will be split by population and need.
The money could charter smaller planes that bring providers in and take patients out, filling every seat, and return patients the same day.
This pilot covers planned, non-emergency care; emergencies are a separate problem tied to statewide bed and doctor shortages, but will be added to the list.
Staff met many carriers, including one with a wheelchair ramp, and the community will need to weigh options such as a runway extension.
No commercial airline can give medical help in flight; only air ambulance services or the Air National Guard can.

parts.title: Questions: federal subsidy, insurance and who will run it

raised.concern: Whether federal Essential Air Service subsidy money can be used for this.
Whether the pilot will produce a data-based report and look at what insurance plans cover for travel, to plan for sustainability.
Someone on Molokaʻi needs to step up to bid on the RFP, and the community should support them.
Molokaʻi's share may be about $1.25 million to cover both the operator and airfares, insurers reimburse little, and the money could run out early.

answered.said: Essential Air Service is federal money; Molokaʻi qualifies but has no subsidy because the route is still profitable, so the congressional delegation would need to help.
Mokulele's 14 scheduled flights block the subsidy and only the airline can complain; legislators asked the congressional delegation to seek an exemption.
Some residents have no insurance, so reimbursement must be considered; a health plan could even bid on the program.
The contractor must collect data from patients and providers, and a rural health policy research center will help write a report for the Legislature.
The RFP is open to any qualified bidder by law, but she hopes a Molokaʻi organization applies.
Legislators cannot change insurer rules; the concern will be written down for the team to consider.
Insurer reimbursement problems were also heard on Lānaʻi; they cannot be fixed through this program but may be addressed in separate policy.

parts.title: Community remarks and questions on program design

raised.concern: The operator must be well connected in health care and able to act as travel agent and coordinator with providers, insurers and patients, including privacy rules; Molokaʻi General Hospital may be the only local group with that capacity.
Asked for a document that lets medical travelers skip airport security screening.
Who will process and receive insurance reimbursement, the operator or patients, given that 65 to 70 percent of the island is on Med-QUEST.
How success will be measured: number of flights or real health outcomes.
Details on the charter planes being considered.
Focusing on kūpuna could make the money last longer; everyone should fill out the surveys.
What is known about which care people leave for, what could come to the island, and who pays out of pocket.

answered.said: Legislators do not control airport security or customs; that could be raised later with Congress.
These details, including confidentiality, will be added to the RFP.
Better health outcomes would be ideal, but staff must check with data experts on whether that can be measured.
Small charter planes in Hawaiʻi are one option among any carriers; wheelchair access remains a challenge, and the operator must build its own carrier relationships.
A hospital with patient histories could help set priorities, and whoever runs the program will have support.

parts.title: Closing and survey deadline
parts.presenter: State Senator, State Representative and Department of Health program specialist
presented: Legislators thanked the community and said they will stay on the issue.
Residents set this Friday as the deadline for survey responses.
Providers who have not met Department of Health staff can do so before they leave Thursday.

bills.name: Request for proposals for non-emergency medical air transportation
bills.what: Will hire entities to buy plane seats for patients and bring providers to Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi.

open_questions.question: How much of the pilot money will Molokaʻi receive?
Who will process and receive insurance reimbursements under the pilot, and what happens if the money runs out early?
Can Molokaʻi get an exemption to receive Essential Air Service subsidy for other airlines?
How will the pilot's success be measured?
